question: Based on the abovementioned results, explain why pseudogenes evolve faster than their functional counterparts and why this pattern is different for the third position in codons.
student_answer: If a functional gene has a significant effect on the fitness, it will be under the influence of selection. The reason is that a deleterous or otherwise harmful mutation inside this gene can result in the inability to produce the protein the gene codes for. Organisms with these mutations will thus have a decreased fitness, if they are even viable at all, depending on the importance of this protein for this organism. Only mutations that are neutral (synonymous) or beneficial are thus expected to be able to accumulate over time as any individual with non-synonymous mutations will be strongly selected against. In contrast, a pseudogene is thought to have lost its function. This means that any kind of mutation that might occur, will have virtually no effect. Whether that mutation is synonymous or non-synonymous, it does not influence the fitness of the organism, and thus mutations are free to accumulate over time.*It is interesting to note here that because of gene duplication, it is possible for one gene to accumulate disadvantageous mutations as its counterpart is enough to take over its function allowing for the continuation of the production of the protein in question. In certain situations, the other gene can thus become a pseudogene.*As for why the third position of a codon does not differ as much in number of accumulated mutations, one has to understand that there are many more codons than amino acids. In practise this means that multiple different codons often encode for the same amino acid. The first and second position are most important for determining the identity of amino acid it translates to, but the third base often has little influence. This allows for more freedom for synonymous mutations to occur at the third position than at the first or second.
